items.stem: In 2014, India’s Supreme Court (NALSA v Union of India) recognised…
options: transgender people as a “third gender” with constitutional rights
same-sex marriage
a separate electorate for religious minorities
Hindi as the sole official language
items.answer: transgender people as a “third gender” with constitutional rights
items.markingKey: A. The ruling required the state to recognise self-identified gender and provide affirmative measures.

items.stem: "A nation and a state are the same thing." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: A state is a political and legal entity with sovereignty over territory; a nation is a community of shared identity. Some nations lack states (e.g. Kurds), and many states contain several nations.
items.markingKey: A state is a political and legal entity with sovereignty over territory; a nation is a community of shared identity. Some nations lack states (e.g. Kurds), and many states contain several nations. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between civic nationalism and ethnic nationalism.
items.answer: Civic nationalism bases membership on shared citizenship and political values, open to newcomers; ethnic nationalism bases membership on descent, language or culture, and is more exclusive.
items.markingKey: Civic nationalism bases membership on shared citizenship and political values, open to newcomers; ethnic nationalism bases membership on descent, language or culture, and is more exclusive. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem:
Source C
The nation is an imagined political community. It is imagined because the members of even the smallest nation will never know most of their fellow members, yet in the minds of each lives the image of their communion.
— Benedict Anderson, Imagined Communities (1983) (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source C, explain how the source supports a constructivist view of national identity. [3]
items.answer: It argues that the nation exists through shared imagination rather than natural ties, so national identity is socially constructed and can change over time.

ethnic nationalism

items.stem: Explain why constructivists argue that ethnic identities are not fixed.
items.answer: Identities change over time and are shaped by institutions, colonial policies and elites; for example, Belgian colonial rule in Rwanda made Hutu and Tutsi categories rigid through identity cards from 1933.

items.stem: With reference to India’s Citizenship Amendment Act (2019), explain how it illustrates religion and national identity.
items.answer: The Act offered a faster route to citizenship for non-Muslim migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan, triggering large protests over whether it made religion a criterion of citizenship. The debate reflected competing visions of Indian national identity – secular and civic versus religious – showing how citizenship law expresses identity politics.
items.markingKey: Context (The Act offered a faster route to citizenship for non-Muslim migrants from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan, triggering large protests over whether it made religion a criterion of citizenship.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: The debate reflected competing visions of Indian national identity – secular and civic versus religious – showing how citizenship law expresses identity politics. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to religion and national identity.

items.stem: "Identity has become more important than economic interest in shaping contemporary politics." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Identity has grown in salience, but it is intertwined with economic interest rather than replacing it.

items.stem: Explain why some states resist minority claims for recognition.
items.answer: Governments may fear that recognition will encourage secession, weaken national unity, require costly redistribution of land and resources, or challenge the dominant group’s identity.

items.stem: With reference to the Rohingya of Myanmar, explain how it illustrates identity-based exclusion and statelessness.
items.answer: Denied citizenship by the 1982 Citizenship Law and subjected to restrictions, more than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh after military operations in 2017; a case under the Genocide Convention is before the ICJ. Exclusion from citizenship on the basis of identity removed legal protection and preceded mass displacement, showing the consequences of non-recognition.

items.stem: Outline two points that could be used to evaluate the claim: "Claims for recognition by Indigenous peoples are best met through autonomy within existing states."
items.answer: Autonomy is the most realistic route, but it is meaningful only when it includes control over land and resources.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Sámi parliaments, Nunavut; territorial integrity norms; UNDRIP frames self-determination as autonomy. Arguments against: autonomy without land control is limited; states can override autonomy (mining, wind farms); some groups seek stronger forms of sovereignty. Supported judgement: Autonomy is the most realistic route, but it is meaningful only when it includes control over land and resources.

items.stem: Which author argued in What Is Populism? (2016) that populism is essentially anti-pluralist?
items.answer: Jan-Werner Müller

items.stem: Explain why economic explanations of populism are contested.
items.answer: Economic insecurity after the 2008 crisis and globalisation help explain support, but many populist voters are not the poorest, and cultural attitudes to immigration and social change predict support strongly, so cultural factors also matter.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: Economic insecurity after the 2008 crisis and globalisation help explain support, but many populist voters are not the poorest, and cultural attitudes to immigration and social change predict support strongly, so cultural factors also matter. items.stem: "Populist parties win mainly because of poor voters." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: Support comes from across income groups; education, age and cultural attitudes are often stronger predictors than income alone.
items.markingKey: Support comes from across income groups; education, age and cultural attitudes are often stronger predictors than income alone. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Hungary under Viktor Orbán (since 2010), explain how it illustrates populism and democratic backsliding.
items.answer: Fidesz used its two-thirds majority to rewrite the constitution, reshape the courts and media regulator, and present the government as the defender of national and Christian identity; the European Parliament described Hungary in 2022 as an “electoral autocracy”. An elected government used its mandate to weaken checks and balances, illustrating how populism can erode liberal democracy from within.
items.markingKey: Context (Fidesz used its two-thirds majority to rewrite the constitution, reshape the courts and media regulator, and present the government as the defender of national and Christian identity; the European Parliament described Hungary in 2022 as an “electoral autocracy”.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: An elected government used its mandate to weaken checks and balances, illustrating how populism can erode liberal democracy from within. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to populism and democratic backsliding.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Populism is a greater threat to democracy than authoritarianism."
items.answer: Populism is a distinctive threat because it hollows out democracy legally, though it is less extreme than outright authoritarianism.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: erodes democracy from within through elections (Hungary); harder to resist because it claims legitimacy; polarisation. Arguments against: outright authoritarian regimes deny rights more completely; populism can be removed by elections (Poland 2023); can increase participation. Supported judgement: Populism is a distinctive threat because it hollows out democracy legally, though it is less extreme than outright authoritarianism.

items.stem: Which political scientist defined populism as a “thin-centred ideology” opposing the pure people to the corrupt elite?

Francis Fukuyama
Cas Mudde
Robert Putnam
items.answer: Cas Mudde
items.markingKey: C. Mudde’s definition (2004) is the most widely used in comparative research.

items.stem: Distinguish between liberal democracy and illiberal democracy.
items.answer: Liberal democracy combines elections with rule of law, protection of rights and independent institutions; illiberal democracy keeps elections but erodes these liberal protections.

items.answer: Left-wing populism defines the elite mainly in economic terms and the people inclusively (Podemos, Syriza); right-wing populism adds an exclusionary cultural or national dimension that targets migrants or minorities (National Rally, Fidesz).

items.answer: Indigenous peoples seek to be heard, not only counted; a First Nations Voice in the constitution; a commission for agreement-making and truth-telling
items.markingKey: Award 1 mark for each of the following, up to [3]: Indigenous peoples seek to be heard, not only counted; a First Nations Voice in the constitution; a commission for agreement-making and truth-telling. items.stem: Outline one way in which the Catalan independence movement (2017) shows nationalism and the challenge to state sovereignty.
items.answer: Catalonia’s regional government held a referendum ruled unconstitutional; Spain imposed direct rule under Article 155 and several leaders were imprisoned, then pardoned in 2021 and covered by an amnesty law in 2024. A sub-state nation claimed self-determination, while the Spanish state defended territorial integrity and constitutional legitimacy.
items.markingKey: Context (Catalonia’s regional government held a referendum ruled unconstitutional; Spain imposed direct rule under Article 155 and several leaders were imprisoned, then pardoned in 2021 and covered by an amnesty law in 2024.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. Link: A sub-state nation claimed self-determination, while the Spanish state defended territorial integrity and constitutional legitimacy. – remaining marks for explicitly connecting the example to nationalism and the challenge to state sovereignty.

items.stem:
Source A
Populists claim that they, and only they, represent the true people. All other political competitors are essentially illegitimate, and anyone who does not support the populists might not be part of the people at all. Populism is therefore always anti-pluralist.
— Jan-Werner Müller, What Is Populism? (2016) (paraphrased)

Using evidence from Source A, explain how the source suggests populism threatens democracy. [4]
items.answer: If only the populist represents the people, opponents, minorities and independent institutions are delegitimised, undermining the pluralism and peaceful competition on which democracy depends.
items.markingKey: If only the populist represents the people, opponents, minorities and independent institutions are delegitimised, undermining the pluralism and peaceful competition on which democracy depends. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: A student claims: "Recognising minority languages always weakens national unity." Identify the error in this claim and correct it.
items.answer: Accommodation can strengthen loyalty to the state, as with official multilingualism in Switzerland and language rights in Canada; denial of recognition has more often fuelled conflict.
items.markingKey: Accommodation can strengthen loyalty to the state, as with official multilingualism in Switzerland and language rights in Canada; denial of recognition has more often fuelled conflict. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Analyse one strength and one limitation of this view: "Nationalism is a greater threat to peace than to democracy."
items.answer: Nationalism threatens both when ethnically exclusive, but civic forms can sustain both peace and democracy.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: secessionist and interstate conflicts; Russia’s nationalist justifications in Ukraine; ethnic nationalism in the Balkans. Arguments against: nationalism can underpin democratic citizenship; exclusionary nationalism erodes minority rights and democracy; peaceful nationalisms (Scotland 2014). Supported judgement: Nationalism threatens both when ethnically exclusive, but civic forms can sustain both peace and democracy.

items.stem: "Populism is a greater threat to democracy than authoritarianism." With reference to specific examples, discuss this statement. [15]
items.answer: Populism is a distinctive threat because it hollows out democracy legally, though it is less extreme than outright authoritarianism.
items.markingKey: Indicative content – arguments for: erodes democracy from within through elections (Hungary); harder to resist because it claims legitimacy; polarisation. Arguments against: outright authoritarian regimes deny rights more completely; populism can be removed by elections (Poland 2023); can increase participation. Possible judgement: Populism is a distinctive threat because it hollows out democracy legally, though it is less extreme than outright authoritarianism. items.stem: Evaluate the claim: "Claims for recognition by Indigenous peoples are best met through autonomy within existing states."
items.answer: Autonomy is the most realistic route, but it is meaningful only when it includes control over land and resources.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: Sámi parliaments, Nunavut; territorial integrity norms; UNDRIP frames self-determination as autonomy. Arguments against: autonomy without land control is limited; states can override autonomy (mining, wind farms); some groups seek stronger forms of sovereignty. Supported judgement: Autonomy is the most realistic route, but it is meaningful only when it includes control over land and resources. items.stem:
Source D
Identity is not destiny. Each person has many identities – of nationality, religion, language, profession, gender and politics. Reducing people to a single identity, such as their religion or civilisation, encourages conflict by making division appear inevitable.
— Amartya Sen, Identity and Violence (2006) (paraphrased)

With reference to Source D, explain how the source challenges the idea of a “clash of civilisations”. [4]
items.answer: By stressing multiple, overlapping identities, it rejects Huntington’s treatment of civilisations as fixed blocs, arguing that the single-identity view itself helps create conflict.
items.markingKey: By stressing multiple, overlapping identities, it rejects Huntington’s treatment of civilisations as fixed blocs, arguing that the single-identity view itself helps create conflict. 3–4 marks: clear explanation with explicit, relevant reference to the source and accurate use of concepts; 1–2 marks: limited explanation, or quotation/description without explanation.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "Indigenous peoples"?
options: The gradual erosion of democratic institutions and norms by elected governments, such as weakening courts, media and electoral fairness

Peoples descended from those who inhabited a territory before colonisation or the formation of the present state, who retain distinct social, cultural and political institutions and self-identify as Indigenous
The belief that a nation – a group sharing a sense of common identity – should have its own state or political self-government, and the political movements based on that belief

The right of peoples to freely determine their political status and pursue their economic, social and cultural development; for Indigenous peoples it is usually exercised through autonomy within existing states
items.answer: Peoples descended from those who inhabited a territory before colonisation or the formation of the present state, who retain distinct social, cultural and political institutions and self-identify as Indigenous
items.markingKey: B. "Indigenous peoples" is peoples descended from those who inhabited a territory before colonisation or the formation of the present state, who retain distinct social, cultural and political institutions and self-identify as Indigenous.

items.stem: Which of the following best describes "civic nationalism"?
options: A form of nationalism based on shared citizenship, institutions and political values, open in principle to anyone who accepts them
Charles Taylor’s (1992) argument that identity is shaped by recognition from others, so misrecognition or non-recognition of a group can be a form of oppression

The right of peoples to freely determine their political status and pursue their economic, social and cultural development; for Indigenous peoples it is usually exercised through autonomy within existing states

A regime that holds elections but restricts liberal features such as judicial independence, media freedom and minority rights; a term popularised by Fareed Zakaria (1997) and embraced by Viktor Orbán in 2014
items.answer: A form of nationalism based on shared citizenship, institutions and political values, open in principle to anyone who accepts them
items.markingKey: A. "civic nationalism" is a form of nationalism based on shared citizenship, institutions and political values, open in principle to anyone who accepts them.

items.stem: State what is meant by the term "illiberal democracy".
items.answer: A regime that holds elections but restricts liberal features such as judicial independence, media freedom and minority rights; a term popularised by Fareed Zakaria (1997) and embraced by Viktor Orbán in 2014
items.markingKey: 1 mark for the core idea: a regime that holds elections but restricts liberal features such as judicial independence, media freedom and minority rights; a term popularised by Fareed Zakaria (1997) and embraced by Viktor Orbán in 2014. Award full marks only if the defining feature is clear; a vague example alone scores 0.

items.stem: Distinguish between redistribution and recognition.
items.answer: Recognition addresses cultural injustice – status, respect and identity; redistribution addresses economic injustice – income, land and resources (Fraser).
items.markingKey: Recognition addresses cultural injustice – status, respect and identity; redistribution addresses economic injustice – income, land and resources (Fraser). One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Distinguish between primordialism and constructivism.
items.answer: Primordialism sees ethnic and national identities as ancient, natural and fixed; constructivism sees them as socially created, changing and open to political mobilisation.
items.markingKey: Primordialism sees ethnic and national identities as ancient, natural and fixed; constructivism sees them as socially created, changing and open to political mobilisation. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Yusuf writes: "Populist parties win mainly because of poor voters." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Support comes from across income groups; education, age and cultural attitudes are often stronger predictors than income alone.
items.markingKey: Support comes from across income groups; education, age and cultural attitudes are often stronger predictors than income alone. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Distinguish between a minority and an Indigenous people.
items.answer: A minority is a numerically smaller, non-dominant group distinguished by ethnicity, religion or language; Indigenous peoples have a historical continuity with pre-colonial societies and a special relationship to land, and claim rights such as self-determination and FPIC.
items.markingKey: A minority is a numerically smaller, non-dominant group distinguished by ethnicity, religion or language; Indigenous peoples have a historical continuity with pre-colonial societies and a special relationship to land, and claim rights such as self-determination and FPIC. One mark for a correct account of each side; further marks for making the difference explicit (not two separate definitions).

items.stem: Briefly explain why nationalism can be both a unifying and a divisive force.
items.answer: It can unite diverse people around common institutions and anti-colonial struggles (India, 1947), but it can also exclude minorities and fuel secessionist or interstate conflict when the nation is defined ethnically.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It can unite diverse people around common institutions and anti-colonial struggles (India, 1947), but it can also exclude minorities and fuel secessionist or interstate conflict when the nation is defined ethnically. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Explain why populism can be seen as both a threat and a corrective to democracy.
items.answer: It can give voice to excluded groups and challenge unresponsive elites, increasing participation, but its anti-pluralism can erode minority rights, checks and balances and the legitimacy of opposition.
items.markingKey: Award marks for: It can give voice to excluded groups and challenge unresponsive elites, increasing participation, but its anti-pluralism can erode minority rights, checks and balances and the legitimacy of opposition. (2 marks: one for each linked point in the chain of reasoning; no marks for assertion without explanation.)

items.stem: Outline one way in which the Australian Voice referendum (2023) shows claims for recognition in a democracy.
items.answer: The proposal to establish an advisory Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice to Parliament was rejected by about 60 per cent of voters, despite support from many Indigenous leaders who had issued the Uluru Statement from the Heart (2017). Indigenous claims for constitutional recognition depended on majority approval, showing the challenge of securing minority recognition through majoritarian processes.
items.markingKey: Context (The proposal to establish an advisory Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Voice to Parliament was rejected by about 60 per cent of voters, despite support from many Indigenous leaders who had issued the Uluru Statement from the Heart (2017).) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. The nation is an imagined political community. It is imagined because the members of even the smallest nation will never know most of their fellow members, yet in the minds of each lives the image of their communion.

Outline three points made in Source D about identity and politics. [3]
items.answer: it is an imagined political community; members will never know most fellow members; members nonetheless share an image of communion

items.stem: Briefly describe the Rohingya of Myanmar and explain what it reveals about identity-based exclusion and statelessness.
items.answer: Denied citizenship by the 1982 Citizenship Law and subjected to restrictions, more than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh after military operations in 2017; a case under the Genocide Convention is before the ICJ. Exclusion from citizenship on the basis of identity removed legal protection and preceded mass displacement, showing the consequences of non-recognition.
items.markingKey: Context (Denied citizenship by the 1982 Citizenship Law and subjected to restrictions, more than 700,000 Rohingya fled to Bangladesh after military operations in 2017; a case under the Genocide Convention is before the ICJ.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: Kenji writes: "Ethnic conflicts are caused by ancient hatreds between groups." Explain why this is inaccurate.
items.answer: Most scholars argue that conflicts arise from political competition, inequality and elite mobilisation; groups have often coexisted peacefully for long periods.
items.markingKey: Most scholars argue that conflicts arise from political competition, inequality and elite mobilisation; groups have often coexisted peacefully for long periods. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: With reference to Brexit (2016), explain how it illustrates identity, sovereignty and populism.
items.answer: The Leave campaign’s slogan “Take Back Control” combined sovereignty, immigration and anti-elite themes; the vote divided the UK by age, education and region. The campaign mobilised national identity and distrust of distant elites, showing how populist themes shape referendums.
items.markingKey: Context (The Leave campaign’s slogan “Take Back Control” combined sovereignty, immigration and anti-elite themes; the vote divided the UK by age, education and region.) – 1 mark for accurate, specific detail. items.stem: "UNDRIP is a legally binding treaty." Explain the flaw in this statement.
items.answer: UNDRIP is a General Assembly declaration and not legally binding, though some states (e.g. Canada in 2021, Bolivia in 2007) have incorporated it into domestic law.
items.markingKey: UNDRIP is a General Assembly declaration and not legally binding, though some states (e.g. Canada in 2021, Bolivia in 2007) have incorporated it into domestic law. 1 mark for identifying the error, 1-2 marks for the correct explanation.

items.stem: Give one argument for and one argument against this view: "Identity has become more important than economic interest in shaping contemporary politics."
items.answer: Identity has grown in salience, but it is intertwined with economic interest rather than replacing it.
items.markingKey: Arguments for: rise of identity-based voting (Brexit, populism); nationalist and religious mobilisation; conflicts over gender and recognition. Arguments against: economic grievances underpin identity politics; class still structures voting; identity often mobilised for material ends. Supported judgement: Identity has grown in salience, but it is intertwined with economic interest rather than replacing it.
